1342907300.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The red highlighted line marks the shorter, concave right and superior border of the stomach extending from the cardiac orifice to the pylorus, which provides attachment to the lesser omentum (hepatogastric and hepatoduodenal ligaments).
1342907300.keyConcept: The lesser curvature forms the concave postero-superior/right border of the stomach and gives attachment to the lesser omentum; it contains the incisura angularis and is supplied by the anastomosing right and left gastric arteries.

99066875.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The red arrow points to the distal, tubular, narrow segment (approximately 2–3 cm long) of the pyloric region of the stomach that leads directly into the duodenum at the pyloric constriction.
99066875.keyConcept: The pyloric region is divided into a wider proximal pyloric antrum and a narrower distal pyloric canal; the canal ends at the pyloric sphincter (gastroduodenal junction).

443785901.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The red arrow points to the broad, expanded proximal chamber of the pyloric region located between the incisura angularis (demarcating the body) and the distal tubular pyloric canal.
443785901.keyConcept: The pyloric antrum is the wider proximal division of the pyloric part of the stomach; it contains endocrine G-cells secreting gastrin and produces forceful peristaltic mixing waves.

1816534874.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The red arrow identifies the central, largest region of the stomach situated between the horizontal plane through the cardiac notch (separating the fundus above) and the oblique plane through the angular incisure (separating the pyloric antrum below).
1816534874.keyConcept: The body of the stomach represents its largest anatomical division, lined by prominent rugae and containing gastric glands rich in parietal (oxyntic) and chief (peptic) cells.

189217298.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The red line highlights the greater curvature of the stomach, which serves as the site of attachment for the greater omentum, an extensive double sheet of peritoneum (four layers) derived embryologically from the dorsal mesentery (dorsal mesogastrium).
189217298.keyConcept: The greater omentum suspends from the greater curvature of the stomach and transverse colon, derived from the dorsal mesentery; it wraps around intra-abdominal inflammatory foci ('policeman of the abdomen').

48588261.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The red line highlights the lesser curvature of the stomach, which gives attachment to the lesser omentum (hepatogastric and hepatoduodenal ligaments), derived embryologically from the ventral mesentery (ventral mesogastrium).
48588261.keyConcept: The lesser omentum connects the lesser curvature of the stomach and the first part of the duodenum to the liver; derived from embryonic ventral mesentery, its free margin encloses the portal triad.

2128060054.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The red arrow points to the uncinate process, a hook-shaped projection extending medially and superiorly from the inferior part of the head of the pancreas, situated posterior to the superior mesenteric vessels.
2128060054.keyConcept: The uncinate process of the pancreas develops from the ventral pancreatic bud; it extends medially behind the superior mesenteric vessels (SMA and SMV) and rests posteriorly on the abdominal aorta.

979550721.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The red arrow points to the head of the pancreas, the expanded disc-shaped right extremity of the pancreas firmly nestled within the C-shaped concavity of the duodenum.
979550721.keyConcept: The head of the pancreas lies within the C-loop of the duodenum anterior to the IVC and renal veins; tumors here frequently compress the common bile duct, causing painless obstructive jaundice.

47302193.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The red arrow points to the constricted neck of the pancreas (about 2 cm in length) connecting the head to the body, lying directly anterior to the superior mesenteric vessels and origin of the portal vein.
47302193.keyConcept: The neck of the pancreas bridges the head and body; posteriorly, the superior mesenteric vein joins the splenic vein to form the portal vein directly behind the pancreatic neck.

423019598.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The red arrow points to the elongated, prismatic body of the pancreas extending obliquely to the left across the abdominal aorta, L2 vertebra, and left kidney towards the spleen.
423019598.keyConcept: The body of the pancreas forms part of the stomach bed, separated from the stomach by the lesser sac (omental bursa); the splenic artery runs tortuously along its superior border.

81221660.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The red arrow points to the narrow, tapered left tip of the pancreas, which extends into the splenorenal (lienorenal) ligament to reach the hilum of the spleen.
81221660.keyConcept: The tail of the pancreas is the only intraperitoneal part of the organ, situated within the splenorenal ligament alongside the splenic vessels; it contains the highest relative density of islets of Langerhans.

1651107801.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The black arrow enters the epiploic foramen (foramen of Winslow), the natural aperture communicating between the greater peritoneal sac and the lesser sac (omental bursa), situated directly posterior to the free right margin of the lesser omentum.
1651107801.keyConcept: The epiploic foramen is bounded anteriorly by the portal triad (bile duct, hepatic artery proper, portal vein) in the hepatoduodenal ligament, posteriorly by the IVC, superiorly by the caudate lobe of the liver, and inferiorly by the first part of the duodenum.

1842229003.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The teal arrow (label 11) points to the anal canal, the terminal 3–4 cm of the large intestine extending from the anorectal junction through the pelvic diaphragm/perineum to the external anal orifice.
1842229003.keyConcept: The anal canal begins at the anorectal junction where the rectum pierces the levator ani; it features the pectinate line dividing neurovascular and lymphatic drainage into somatic and visceral territories.

1486756612.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The teal arrow (label 10) points to the rectum, the pelvic portion of the large intestine between the sigmoid colon (at S3 level) and the anal canal, characterized by a smooth external surface lacking haustra, taeniae, or appendices epiploicae.
1486756612.keyConcept: The rectum extends from S3 to the pelvic diaphragm; it possesses three lateral curvatures marked internally by transverse rectal folds (valves of Houston) and dilates inferiorly to form the rectal ampulla.

1997037689.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Label 2 points to the vermiform appendix, a narrow, blind-ended tubular diverticulum originating from the posteromedial caecal wall at the convergence of the three taeniae coli, approximately 2 cm below the ileocaecal valve.
1997037689.keyConcept: The vermiform appendix contains abundant lymphoid follicles in its submucosa and is suspended by the mesoappendix carrying the appendicular artery (a branch of the ileocolic artery); its anatomical base is reliably found at the confluence of the three taeniae coli.

1479153172.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Label 1 points to the terminal ileum as it approaches and enters the medial wall of the caecum at the ileocaecal junction.
1479153172.keyConcept: The terminal ileum enters the caecum at the ileocaecal junction, flanked by superior and inferior ileocaecal lips that form the ileocaecal valve, regulating emptying and preventing retrograde colonic reflux.

263295419.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Label 1 points to loops of jejunum located predominantly in the upper left infragolic compartment; corroborated by the inset displaying prominent, dense circular mucosal folds (plicae circulares), simple arterial arcades (1–2 tiers), and long straight vasa recta.
263295419.keyConcept: The jejunum comprises the proximal two-fifths of the small intestine following the duodenum; characterized by a wider caliber, thicker wall, prominent plicae circulares, tall vasa recta, and less mesenteric fat compared to the ileum.

581115387.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Label 2 points to loops of ileum situated primarily in the lower right infragolic compartment and pelvis; corroborated by the inset showing multiple complex arterial arcade tiers (3–4 tiers), short vasa recta, abundant mesenteric fat encroaching onto the intestinal border, and sparse plicae circulares.
581115387.keyConcept: The ileum forms the distal three-fifths of the small intestine; distinguished by abundant mesenteric fat extending up to the intestinal wall, short vasa recta arising from multi-tiered arcades, and aggregated lymphoid nodules (Peyer's patches).

1880786057.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Label 7 points to the transverse mesocolon, the broad peritoneal fold connecting the transverse colon to the posterior abdominal wall along the anterior border of the pancreas.
1880786057.keyConcept: The transverse mesocolon conveys the middle colic vessels to the transverse colon; its horizontal root divides the abdominal cavity into supracolic and infracolic compartments.

1738073804.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Label 6 points to the greater omentum, shown here reflected superiorly over the costal margin; it is the extensive peritoneal apron attached to the greater curvature of the stomach and transverse colon.
1738073804.keyConcept: The greater omentum is a four-layered fold of peritoneum containing fat and milky spots (macrophage aggregates); it drapes over the small intestine and adheres to inflamed areas to prevent peritonitis.
